newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dell ups Europe share, eyes online commerce.
newsitem.headline: Dell ups Europe share, eyes online commerce.

text.p: PC maker Dell Computer Corp said on Thursday it posted sizable first-quarter gains in Britain, France and Germany as its share of Europe's personal computer market climbed 2.2 percentage points to 5.8 percent.
The company's German unit also said it was ramping up Internet-based sales systems that should reduce costs and push the direct marketer ahead of competitiors in online commerce.

The online systems and increasing European acceptance of credit card and direct sales should also keep Dell growing strongly in 1997, said Hans-Juergen Mammitzsch, managing director of Dell Computer GmbH, said.
"Things are going in our direction," he told Reuters after a news conference. "We are in a good position to see growth in Europe the rest of the year."

The company on Tuesday announced first-quarter European sales rose 38 percent to $644 million as worldwide sales soared 58 percent to $2.6 billion, a figure that made Dell the world's third largest PC maker.
Dell declined to break out European results further, but on Thursday provided market research figures that Mammitzsch called "pretty accurate".

In unit sales, Dell boosted its share of the British market to 12.8 percent, up from 9.5 percent in the first quarter of 1996, according to International Data Corp. (IDC). In France, Dell's share in the quarter reached 5.4 percent, compared to 3.5 percent a year ago. In Germany, it was 3.3 percent, up from 2.6 percent.
Dell has been able to compete on price and gain share because its direct sales model eliminates many inventory costs involved in selling through computer resellers, said IDC analyst Bruce Stephen.
"They are the business process champions, the envy of the industry with their quick inventory turns," he said. "The credibility of their direct model seems to be taking hold globally."

To maintain momentum, Dell was pushing into online sales in Europe, following the lead of its U.S. operation, Mammiitzsch said. In Germany, Dell planned start up a system in June that would allow buyers to select from a variety of monitors, hard drives and other options for PCs ordered electronically.
Right now, buyers choose from a limited range of standard PC configurations displayed on Dell's German Internet site and on T-Online, the leading online service in Germany.

T-Online sales and the two-month old German Internet sales site combined to generate about $1.3 million in sales in April. Mammitzsch expected online sales to account for about five percent of total sales by the end of 1997.
By the fourth quarter, Dell would add an online system that gives customers order status and shipment information, and planned to have sales sites on the internal networks of several large customers.
"They are on the forefront of creating customer linkages that can be very powerful tools for selling software upgrades and other products beyond PCs," Stephen said.

At the same time, Dell expected to reduce sales costs. In online sales, it requires an average of 0.5 phone calls to turn a sales lead into a purchase, he said. Traditional media like magazine advertisements require 4.5 calls on average.
Dell offered 30,000 pages of technical information on its Internet site to enable customers to get answers to many questions without calling Dell support lines, Mammitzsch said.
"If you reduce the number of calls that come in, the effect on productivity is incredible," Mammitzsch said.
